title: Momentum
tagline: Ranking past winners, the skip-month, dual momentum, calendars, crashes and other asset classes
summary: Momentum is two hypotheses that share a name. Cross-sectional momentum ranks assets by past return and holds the winners against the losers. Time-series momentum, already met as trend, looks only at an asset’s own past. This course builds the ranking, the skip-month, dual momentum and calendar rotation, then studies the crash, and finally asks what happens when the same sentences are applied to FX.
overview: Jegadeesh and Titman formed portfolios on the past three to twelve months of stock returns, skipped a short gap, and held them for a similar horizon. Winners continued to beat losers on average in their sample. That is cross-sectional momentum. It needs a universe and a ranking. It is not the same object as a single ETF crossing its own moving average, even though both are called momentum in casual speech. This course keeps the two names apart.

Implementation choices move the result as much as the hypothesis does. Skipping the most recent month avoids a short-horizon reversal that can contaminate a twelve-month ranking. Rebalancing on a calendar, on a drift band, or only when a signal flips are three different turnover policies. Dual momentum adds an absolute filter: hold the relative winner only if its own past return is positive, otherwise hold cash. Each of these is a different experiment. The library’s quarterly dual-momentum example and its monthly rotation example are worked as cases, with their reported summaries attached to the specification rather than to the word 'momentum'.

The crash chapter is not optional. Momentum portfolios have had concentrated left-tail losses, particularly when the market rebounds after a panic and yesterday’s losers lead. A high average return with a severe conditional crash is a different fact from a high Sharpe ratio in a quiet window.

The last chapter takes the same specifications outside equities. Several published FX examples in the library lost money over the window they report. A negative published result is part of the record. It is not an instruction to take the opposite trade.
outcomes: Distinguish cross-sectional momentum from time-series momentum by the information each one uses.
Form a winner-minus-loser portfolio from a past-return ranking and state the formation and holding windows.
Explain the skip-month and an absolute (dual) filter, and compute both on a small cross-section.
Compare calendar rebalancing, drift-band rebalancing and signal-change rebalancing as turnover policies.
Describe momentum crashes as a conditional left tail, not as a reason to discard the average historical result or to trade it.
Read a negative FX momentum backtest as evidence about that specification and sample, not as a forecast of the opposite sign.

history.title: Returns to buying winners and selling losers
history.detail: Jegadeesh and Titman documented intermediate-horizon momentum in US stocks: past winners outperformed past losers over the next three to twelve months in their sample.

history.title: Momentum as a fourth factor
history.detail: Carhart added a winner-minus-loser factor to the Fama–French three-factor model and used it to study mutual-fund performance. The factor is a research instrument, not a product recommendation.

history.title: Value and momentum everywhere
history.detail: Asness, Moskowitz and Pedersen studied value and momentum together across markets and asset classes, and the correlation between them.

history.title: Dual momentum as a book
history.detail: Antonacci’s book popularised the combination of relative momentum across assets and absolute momentum against cash. The library’s quarterly example is one specification in that family, not the book itself.

history.title: Momentum crashes
history.detail: Daniel and Moskowitz showed that momentum strategies have episodic crashes, concentrated in volatile rebounds after declines, and that those crashes account for a large part of the option-like payoff.
